candidate.entry_point: Peer-controlled LoginRequest fields my_id / my_name / session_id (src/client.rs: session_id = rand::random() chosen by the connecting client itself, line ~1844-1857; my_id/my_name are free-form strings set by the caller, line ~2721-2727) reaching server::connection::Connection::handle_login_request2 -> send_logon_response_and_keep_alive (line 1615-1650).

candidate.trace: 1) Legitimate operator connects, supplies correct password + correct TOTP code -> Auth2fa branch (connection.rs:2754-2782) calls raii::AuthedConnID::set_session_2fa(self.session_key()) (line 2765), inserting/marking SESSIONS[{peer_id: their_my_id, name: their_my_name, session_id: their_session_id}].tfa = true; the operator's session stays connected, continuously refreshing session_last_recv_time (line 937). 2) Attacker who has obtained the same current password (phish, credential reuse, keylogger, org-shared permanent password) but does NOT possess the TOTP secret/device opens a second, independent connection and sends a LoginRequest whose my_id/my_name/session_id match the fields the legitimate client used in step 1. 3) validate_password() succeeds (attacker really does know the password) -> send_logon_response_and_keep_alive() is invoked -> is_recent_session(true) finds the SESSIONS entry, sees tfa==true and lr.password non-empty, returns true -> 2FA prompt is skipped entirely -> attacker gets full authorized remote-control access with password alone.
candidate.attack: attacker=holder of a leaked/phished/reused RustDesk password for a 2FA-protected host, exact input=a crafted LoginRequest with my_id/my_name copied from (or coincidentally matching) a currently-active legitimate operator session on that host plus any non-empty password value equal to the current temp/permanent password, observed result=server treats the new unrelated connection as the already-2FA-verified session and grants full authorized access without ever prompting for or checking a TOTP code on this connection.
candidate.preconditions: 2FA must be enabled on the target (require_2fa set) — this is the exact feature meant to stop password-only compromise, so this is a within-threat-model bypass, not out-of-scope. Attacker must also supply the exact (my_id, my_name, session_id) triple used by a legitimate, still-connected (or very recently connected) session; my_id/my_name are attacker-choosable free text with no validation against real identity (my_id in particular is very often shared out-of-band in support scenarios), while session_id is a 64-bit value the legitimate client picks via rand::random() and does not normally transmit anywhere else — this is the main practical brake on exploitation; I found no evidence in the reviewed files that session_id is logged, displayed, or synced anywhere that a remote attacker could read it, so real-world exploitability currently depends on an information leak or a client that uses low-entropy/fixed session_id values, which was not confirmed in-scope.

candidate.disposition_hint: needs-live-validate: confirm in a lab whether any client/CLI/automation surface exposes or fixes session_id (e.g. rustdesk-server-pro API, headless connect flags, ConnToken persistence) before treating this as directly exploitable; if none found, still worth flagging to maintainers as a defense-in-depth gap since the security property '2FA requires possession of the TOTP device on every new connection' is not actually enforced — it is enforced only up to a guessable/knowable non-secret triple.

verdict.reason:
Re-derived end-to-end from raw source, all cited lines verified as claimed.

1. SessionKey (connection.rs:213-217) = {peer_id: String, name: String, session_id: u64} — built purely from `self.lr` fields, and `self.lr = lr.clone()` (line 2450, in handle_login_request_without_validation) is set fresh from whatever LoginRequest the CURRENT connection just sent. No nonce, no signature, no channel-binding, no IP tie (Session struct at 220-224 also carries no IP/peer-conn identity, only last_recv_time/random_password/tfa).

2. is_recent_session(true) (2342-2368) does exactly what's claimed: looks up SESSIONS by self.session_key(), and if found with session.tfa==true and self.lr.password non-empty, returns true — no further crypto check.

3. Confirmed the only reachable path that lets a *new, independent* connection hit is_recent_session(true) and skip 2FA is send_logon_response_and_keep_alive() (1615-1650), called at line 2745 immediately after this connection's OWN validate_password() succeeded (2727), or via 2698 after is_recent_session(false) (temp-password reuse). The Auth2fa success path (2754-2789) that actually calls set_session_2fa (2765) is a *different* connection object populating the SAME cache — confirming cross-connection reuse is the intended read of the code, not a misread. The other two callers of send_logon_response_and_keep_alive (679 Authorize/click-approve, 2821 switch-sides) don't exercise this bypass: 679 already does require_2fa.take() first; 2821 is gated by an independent from_switch flag (a known seed, not this variant).

4. Confirmed the "full session lifetime, not 30s" claim: session_last_recv_time is set to the SESSIONS entry's shared Arc<Mutex<Instant>> at authorization time (1676-1680) and refreshed to Instant::now() on every byte received on ANY connection holding that Arc (line 937), so SESSION_TIMEOUT (30s, line 449) is continuously renewed as long as the original legitimate session stays active — verified via code, not inferred.

5. Rust-layer-only: is_recent_session/session_key/SESSIONS live entirely in src/server/connection.rs backend logic; no Dart/UI involvement in this decision at all — satisfies "verify absent at the RUST layer."

6. Checked the candidate's own stated mitigating factor (session_id secrecy) rather than assuming it: session_id is `rand::random(): u64` in client.rs (1850-1857), and the only export path found is get_conn_token()/ConnToken (client.rs 1726-1730, 2813-2823), exposed to the *local* Dart UI via flutter_ffi session_get_conn_token — used for the client's own restart-remote-device reconnect UX, not transmitted to the server, logged, or exposed to any third party in the files reviewed. This substantiates rather than undercuts the candidate's own caveat — the barrier is real and correctly disclosed as unconfirmed/out-of-scope, not glossed over.

Net: this is a genuine, new SELF-REPORTED-IDENTITY-TRUST variant distinct from the seed (hwid-based trusted-device bypass uses a different field/function, TrustedDevice matching at ~2453, not SessionKey/is_recent_session). The code-level defect — no cryptographic proof ties a SESSIONS cache hit to the connection that actually performed 2FA — is fully provable from source with no unobservable barrier blocking that specific claim. The candidate's own severity (Medium, not High) and confidence (0.5) are already well-calibrated to the one genuinely unverified factor (real-world session_id guessability/leak), so no correction needed.
verdict.live_test: Optional follow-up (not required to confirm the code-level defect): in a 2FA-enabled lab pair, complete a normal login+TOTP from client A, capture its LoginRequest (my_id/my_name/session_id) via a debug build or packet capture, then from a second independent process/socket B send a LoginRequest with the identical my_id/my_name/session_id and a correct password but no Auth2fa message, while A remains connected — expect the server to grant B full access without ever prompting for TOTP. verdict.observed_mitigation: None found for the core bypass mechanism at the Rust layer (no IP/channel-binding, no re-validation of TOTP possession, no nonce). The only real mitigating factor is session_id being a 64-bit rand::random() value whose only located export path (ConnToken via flutter_ffi::session_get_conn_token) is local-client-only and not observed to reach the server, logs, or any third party — this is a genuine but unconfirmed-scope barrier, already disclosed by the candidate, not a reason to reject.

candidate.title: Login-failure lockout is scoped strictly per source IP (/64,/56,/48 for IPv6), giving each distinct source address its own independent guess budget — verified per-IP-only design, distributed brute force feasible against the opt-in low-entropy numeric one-time password

candidate.confidence_reason: The per-IP-only scoping (no global counter for FailureScope::Default) is directly and unambiguously confirmed in source, and directly answers the HUNT LENS's explicit 'per-IP only / distributed bypass' question. candidate.title: aligned_u8_vec allocates with a custom alignment but Vec<u8> always deallocates at align=1 — Vec::from_raw_parts contract violation
candidate.component: hbb_common::mem (consumed by KCP-fed local audio buffer path)
candidate.bug_class: memory-safety / unsound unsafe code (mismatched alloc/dealloc Layout, Vec::from_raw_parts contract violation)
candidate.root_cause: aligned_u8_vec() in libs/hbb_common/src/mem.rs allocates raw memory via std::alloc::alloc(Layout::from_size_align(cap, align)) using a caller-chosen align (4 at its only call site) and then wraps that pointer with Vec::from_raw_parts(ptr, 0, cap). Vec::from_raw_parts's documented safety contract requires the pointer to have been allocated 'with the alignment of T' (T=u8 => align=1). Because Vec<u8>'s Drop/grow paths always recompute the deallocation layout as Layout::array::<u8>(cap) (align=1), every drop of this Vec calls the global allocator's dealloc() with a layout that does not match the layout used at alloc() time. This is undefined behavior per the GlobalAlloc contract, and it is unconditional (present on every call, not merely if the vec is later resized) — the doc-comment on line 1 ('must not be resized or reserverd') only warns about the resize case and misses the deeper always-present alloc/dealloc layout mismatch.
candidate.entry_point: src/server/audio_service.rs:83 pa_impl::align_to_32(), reached from pa_impl::run()'s local `_pa` PulseAudio IPC capture loop (Linux/Android builds only) whenever the captured PCM buffer's pointer happens not to already be 4-byte aligned
candidate.sink: libs/hbb_common/src/mem.rs:12 Vec::from_raw_parts(ptr, 0, cap) inside aligned_u8_vec(), and the implicit dealloc() call later made by that Vec's Drop impl using a mismatched Layout
candidate.trace: audio_service.rs pa_impl::run() reads a PCM buffer over local IPC from the `_pa` pulseaudio helper -> align_to_32(data) checks data.as_ptr() & 3 -> if misaligned, calls hbb_common::mem::aligned_u8_vec(data.len()=3840, 4) -> alloc(Layout{size:3840, align:4}) -> Vec::from_raw_parts(ptr, 0, 3840) (Vec internally assumes align_of::<u8>()==1) -> buf.extend_from_slice(data) fills to full capacity (no resize triggered this call) -> buf is returned up through align_to_32 and eventually dropped by the caller; Vec's Drop computes the dealloc layout as {size:3840, align:1} and frees memory that was actually allocated with align:4.
candidate.attack: Attacker model: a compromised or malicious local process able to write to RustDesk's `_pa` audio IPC channel (the local PulseAudio proxy helper) on a Linux/Android install — not the remote P2P peer. Exact input: a raw PCM buffer of exactly AUDIO_DATA_SIZE_U8 (3840) bytes whose backing allocation the attacker arranges to be non-4-byte-aligned. Observed result: aligned_u8_vec is invoked, producing a Vec<u8> allocated at align=4 but freed by Rust's Vec machinery using align=1 — a documented alloc/dealloc layout mismatch. Linux/Android builds only (`#[cfg(any(target_os = "linux", target_os = "android"))]` gate on pa_impl in audio_service.rs). candidate.confidence_reason: The layout mismatch is unambiguous when read against the documented Vec::from_raw_parts / GlobalAlloc contracts, and it is unconditionally present (not just on a hypothetical future resize) at the sole call site in audio_service.rs. Held at moderate rather than high confidence because: (1) the vec never actually grows beyond its allocated capacity at the current call site, so no double-mismatch abuse is demonstrated live; (2) practical exploitability depends entirely on the target allocator distinguishing align=1 vs align=4 frees, which does not reproduce on default glibc malloc; (3) the reach is local-IPC only, not the remote peer-to-peer/KCP attack surface this hunt is primarily targeting — kcp_stream.rs itself contains no unsafe code, no unmediated buffer math, and correctly orders udp.connect()-before-io-loop plus a KcpPacketHeader-size length gate before ever handing bytes to the KCP endpoint, so it yielded no new memory-safety or permission/identity/secure-channel variant within this file.
candidate.disposition_hint: needs-live-validation-on-allocator (try under Miri or on an Android Scudo build); low remote priority — file as a correctness/soundness fix (allocate via a proper over-aligned-Vec pattern, e.g. Box<[u8]> with manual layout tracking, or a crate like `aligned-vec`) rather than pursuing as a network-facing RCE finding

verdict.reason:
Re-derived from raw mem.rs + audio_service.rs + bytes_codec.rs. The core soundness claim is CONFIRMED as written: aligned_u8_vec() (mem.rs:2-13) does alloc(Layout{size:cap, align}) then Vec::from_raw_parts(ptr,0,cap), and Vec<u8>'s Drop always computes its dealloc layout as Layout::array::<u8>(cap) i.e. align=1 -- a documented violation of Vec::from_raw_parts's safety contract ("T needs to have the same alignment as what ptr was allocated with... the alignment really needs to be equal to satisfy the dealloc requirement"). Sole call site is audio_service.rs:89 (pa_impl::align_to_32, Linux/Android only), align=4, unconditional on every misaligned-buffer call -- verified this part matches the candidate exactly.

Two load-bearing claims in the candidate are wrong and needed correction, one on reachability (upgrade) and one on severity (downgrade):

1. Reachability mischaracterized as attacker-dependent. Candidate frames the trigger as "an attacker arranges" a misaligned buffer via "a compromised or malicious local process." False -- the misalignment is a routine, near-deterministic side effect of hbb_common's own framing, not adversarial input. bytes_codec.rs decode_head() (line 44-74) uses a VARIABLE 1-4 byte header (head_len = (src[0]&0x3)+1) and decode_data() (line 76-81) returns src.split_to(n), a zero-copy view offset into the shared underlying buffer by head_len bytes. Since head_len is not a multiple of 4, ordinary in-protocol audio frames land at non-4-aligned offsets as a matter of course. This fires under completely benign operation any time a peer receives audio from a Linux/Android RustDesk host -- no local attacker, no "arranging," nothing beyond normal voice/audio use.

2. Severity overstated ("Medium potential... allocators that bucket by alignment (Android's Scudo/jemalloc, hardened allocators...) can corrupt heap allocator metadata"). Empirically disproven. Built a byte-for-byte reproduction of aligned_u8_vec(3840,4) + Vec<u8> drop on the reference Linux x86_64 host (root@192.168.1.119, Kali 6.6.15, rustc 1.70.0) and set GDB breakpoints on malloc/free/posix_memalign/aligned_alloc. Result: the align=4 alloc() call resolved to plain MALLOC(size=3840); the later Vec drop (align=1 dealloc) resolved to plain FREE(ptr=<same address>). posix_memalign and aligned_alloc were never invoked anywhere in the trace, and a direct alloc(align=4)/dealloc(align=1) pair behaved identically. This matches Rust std's documented System-allocator MIN_ALIGN fast path (MIN_ALIGN=16 on x86_64/aarch64, 8 on x86/arm -- every architecture RustDesk ships): any Layout.align() <= MIN_ALIGN is silently discarded and the call is dispatched as plain libc malloc()/free() with no alignment argument conveyed at all. Since align=4 <= MIN_ALIGN on every relevant target, the "mismatched" align=4-alloc/align=1-dealloc pair and a "correct" align=1/align=1 pair are LITERALLY the same libc calls -- there is no alignment information left for Scudo/jemalloc/ptmalloc to disagree on, so no heap-metadata corruption occurs on any of RustDesk's actual build targets.

Net: this is a genuine, citable Rust-soundness/lint-class defect (would be flagged by Miri; worth fixing as code hygiene, e.g. switch to Box<[u8]> with tracked layout or the `aligned-vec` crate) but is not a practically exploitable memory-corruption primitive as claimed, and is not attacker-triggered. It also does not match any of the round's four named seed patterns (PERM-GATE-BYPASS / SELF-REPORTED-IDENTITY-TRUST / SECURE-CHANNEL-SKIP / CLIENT-TRUSTS-SERVER-MSG) -- it is an unrelated memory-safety class, out of family for this variant-hunt round, though a legitimate independent finding on its own.

Re-derived from raw source, independent of the candidate's narrative.

1. select_server_uid_for_user_main_ipc (ipc.rs:1242-1272): confirmed the exact code the candidate cites. The three match arms on the deduped/sorted server_uids slice are:

   - `[uid]` (line 1261): `return Ok(*uid)` — unconditional, NO comparison to active_uid() anywhere in this arm.
   - `_` (multi, line 1262+): checks prefer_root, then filters active_uid against the candidate set — DOES check identity.
   The single-candidate arm is provably the only one of the three that skips the active-uid cross-check. This is not a matter of interpretation; it's a direct read of the match arms.

2. Reachability confirmed end-to-end: core_main.rs:207-214 wraps `is_user_main_ipc_scope_cli_command` CLI flags (verified at core_main.rs:912-924 to be exactly `--password/--set-unlock-pin/--get-id/--set-id/--config/--option/--assign/--deploy`, matching the candidate's list) in `UserMainIpcScope::new()`. `connect()` (ipc.rs:1316-1329) checks `geteuid()==0 && postfix.is_empty() && use_user_main_ipc` → calls `user_main_ipc_server_uid()` (ipc.rs:1307) → `running_server_uids_for_current_exe()` (ipc.rs:1275, sysinfo scan for argv[1]=="--server" + canonicalized exe match) → `select_server_uid_for_user_main_ipc`. `--password` (core_main.rs:432-451) and `--config`/`--option` (core_main.rs:496-536) gate only on `is_installed() && is_root()`, then call `ipc::set_permanent_password`/`ipc::set_unlock_pin`/`ui_interface::set_option`, all of which route through `connect(_, "")` — the exact vulnerable path.

3. No server-side compensating control at the Rust layer: `is_service_ipc_postfix()` (hbb_common/config.rs:129-136) explicitly returns false for postfix=="" — only `_service` and `_uinput_*` get `authorize_service_scoped_ipc_connection` (ipc.rs:491-496). The main-IPC listener (postfix "") on Linux/macOS accepts any connecting peer with zero identity check, and `handle()`'s `Data::Config`/`Data::Options` Some-branches (ipc.rs:881-927) apply the value unconditionally. Root also bypasses Unix DAC on the 0700-permissioned socket, so a root client can reach any uid's socket regardless of file permissions. I found no gate anywhere in this chain that re-verifies the selected uid against the real console/active user in the single-candidate case — the permission/auth check the task asked me to verify is genuinely ABSENT at the Rust layer, not merely deferred to Dart/UI.

4. I went further than requested and checked real-world triggerability, which affects severity but not the core claim: on Linux, `start_os_service()` (platform/linux.rs:793-801) calls `stop_rustdesk_servers()` (a `pkill`-style sweep of ALL `--server` processes matching the app name, regardless of uid) at service start and again via `force_stop_server()` whenever `should_start_server()` fires (including an hourly restart), which bounds — but does not eliminate — the attacker's window to be the sole `--server` candidate. On macOS, the equivalent root-driven `--server` management/sweep loop in `platform/macos.rs::start_os_service()` is entirely commented out/dead code, so no such sweep exists there, making the precondition (attacker's `--server` being briefly the only candidate) comparatively easier to hit. This is corroborating evidence, not a mitigation to the code defect itself.

Net: the specific ask — "verify the permission/auth check is ABSENT at the RUST enforcement layer" — is provable from source alone with no unobservable barrier, so this confirms rather than needs-live-validation. The candidate's severity (High, not Critical) and its own "needs-live-validation" disposition_hint for full end-to-end race reproduction are appropriately conservative and I leave them as-is.
verdict.live_test: Two-VM/host reproduction on a Linux install where the rustdesk systemd service is NOT yet running (or has just been stopped) so there is no root-owned or desktop-owned "--server" process: (1) as unprivileged user B, run `/usr/bin/rustdesk --server &`; (2) confirm via `ps -ef | grep -- --server` that B's process is the sole match for that binary; (3) as root run `rustdesk --password 'TESTSECRET123'`; (4) `strace -f -e trace=network,read -p <B_pid>` or inspect B's own `~/.config/<app>/<App>2.toml` afterward to confirm the plaintext password/hash landed in B's config, not the intended target's; (5) confirm root's CLI printed "Done!" despite misrouting. Repeat on macOS (no service-loop sweep present in current source) as the more favorable environment, and repeat with the service actively running (Linux) to confirm the multi-candidate branch's active_uid check causes a safe bail instead — establishing the precise precondition boundary.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None at the Rust layer for the single-candidate branch itself (confirmed absent). Partial real-world exposure-limiting factor found during verification: Linux's start_os_service() sweep (stop_rustdesk_servers()/force_stop_server(), platform/linux.rs:793-801,788-791) periodically kills stray "--server" processes system-wide, narrowing but not closing the attack window; macOS has no such sweep (the equivalent loop in platform/macos.rs is dead/commented-out code), so the precondition is more easily met there.

candidate.title: SSRF / arbitrary internal-network connect via unauthenticated relay_server field from rendezvous server (PunchHoleResponse / RelayResponse)
candidate.root_cause: connect_tcp_local() in socket_client.rs does not validate the `target` host/port (no allowlist, no loopback/link-local/RFC1918/metadata-IP denylist, no check that it matches the configured rendezvous/relay pool) before calling FramedStream::new(target, local, ms_timeout) to open a raw TCP connection, allowing a fully attacker-supplied host:port string to be dialed directly by the victim client.
candidate.entry_point: src/client.rs Client::_start()/_punch_hole path: the rendezvous server's UDP PunchHoleResponse.relay_server (line ~512, `relay_server = ph.relay_server;`) or TCP RelayResponse.relay_server (line ~536-557, `rr.relay_server`) is taken verbatim from an unauthenticated rendezvous-protocol message (obtained via crate::get_next_nonkeyexchange_msg — explicitly pre-key-exchange, i.e. not covered by the NaCl session key) and passed to Client::create_relay().

candidate.attack: Attacker controls (or MITMs, or the victim is pointed at) the rendezvous/ID server. When the victim's RustDesk client attempts to connect to any peer ID, the attacker's server returns PunchHoleResponse.relay_server = "127.0.0.1:8080" or "169.254.169.254:80" or "10.0.0.5:6379" etc. The victim client, with no host-range validation, opens a TCP connection to that internal/loopback/metadata target and sends a RequestRelay protobuf (containing the client's licence_key and target peer id) to it. candidate.preconditions: Requires the client to be configured against (or MITM-reachable via) a malicious/compromised rendezvous ID server — realistic for self-hosted hbbs deployments, or via the already-noted unauth-UDP ConfigureUpdate persistence bug that can repoint rendezvous-servers. candidate.confidence_reason: Code path independently verified end-to-end by reading socket_client.rs and the corresponding client.rs call sites raw; connect_tcp_local performs no target validation whatsoever. verdict.reason: Independently re-read connect_tcp_local (socket_client.rs:150-178) and its callers raw. The absence claim is correct at the Rust enforcement layer: connect_tcp_local performs (a) a SOCKS-proxy check via Config::get_socks(), (b) an IPv4→nip.io rewrite for IPv6-local/IPv4-target mismatch, and nothing else, before calling FramedStream::new(target, local, ms_timeout) at line 175. FramedStream::new (libs/hbb_common/src/tcp.rs:84-111) does a plain lookup_host() + TCP connect with zero destination filtering (no loopback/RFC1918/link-local/169.254.169.254 denylist, no allowlist against configured rendezvous/relay pool). Traced the caller chain end to end: client.rs:512 `relay_server = ph.relay_server` (PunchHoleResponse) and client.rs:556-557 `rr.relay_server` (RelayResponse) are both read via `crate::get_next_nonkeyexchange_msg` (common.rs:1841) off the rendezvous TCP socket. Critically, `secure_tcp()` (which applies RustDesk's NaCl secretbox to that socket) is only invoked at client.rs:429-433 when `!key.is_empty() && !token.is_empty()` — for the default public-server flow (`_start`, client.rs:238-293) key/token are empty, so this rendezvous TCP connection carrying PunchHoleResponse/RelayResponse is genuinely unauthenticated/unencrypted at the wire by default, confirming the candidate's "no crypto proof" framing rather than assuming an unseen secure layer. relay_server then flows unmodified through connect() (client.rs:718-728, request_relay) and create_relay() (client.rs:903-927), where connect_tcp(ipv4_to_ipv6(check_port(relay_server, RELAY_PORT), ipv4), ...) is called at line 911 with zero validation, and RequestRelay{licence_key: key, id: peer, uuid, ...} is sent unconditionally on that raw connection at lines 917-926 — exactly matching the described sink and license-key-leak mechanism. grep across client.rs and the whole call chain turned up no allowlist/denylist/IP-range check on relay_server anywhere (only rendezvous_mediator.rs's separate host-accept path has a *local-config-override* check via get_relay_server, which is a different code path not covered by this candidate and does not contradict it — it too falls through to the unvalidated server-provided value when no local override is set, reinforcing rather than refuting the pattern). This is a genuinely new variant of the established CLIENT-TRUSTS-SERVER-MSG class (distinct sink/mechanism from the ConfigureUpdate seed — raw TCP SSRF-style connect vs config persistence+restart), not a re-report of a seed. All cited line numbers/snippets check out against the current file contents. The only open item is dynamic proof of actual internal-service impact (e.g. successfully reaching a loopback/RFC1918 service and observing effect), which the candidate itself correctly flagged via confidence 0.6 and disposition_hint needs_live_validation rather than over-claiming.
